title: The option for the poor
hookLine: a rich man passes a poor man at his gate every day, and never once sees him

lines: THE POOR MAN HAS A NAME.
cards: A rich man's gate. He goes in and out in purple and fine linen, and feasts every day. At the same gate lies a poor man covered in sores, wishing for the crumbs that fall from the table.
Jesus tells this story in Luke, and two details stand out. The poor man has a name, Lazarus; the rich man never gets one. And the rich man is never cruel.
He doesn't kick Lazarus or send him away. He simply does nothing for him, day after day. Catholic social teaching has a phrase meant to make that kind of passing by hard.
Today, the preferential option for the poor.

teach.b: First, what preferential means here. It doesn't mean God loves poor people more and everyone else less. At a family table, if one child is sick, that child gets served first, and nobody thinks the others are loved less.
The Catechism speaks of the Church's preferential love for those oppressed by poverty in that sense: the ones in greatest need get attention first. Second, where it comes from.

In Luke, Jesus opens his teaching on the plain like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." The Greek word there is ptochos, a word for the poor who depend on others to live.
Not a footnote to the gospel: the first blessing in that sermon. Third, what it isn't.
It isn't meant to set one class against another, and it isn't a task for the poor alone. It's asked of every Christian, rich and poor alike.
John Paul the Second called it a special form of primacy in the exercise of Christian charity. Fourth, how it works.

The phrase gives a lens for judging any decision, from a nation's budget to a parish schedule to a household's spending: how does this land on the people with the least? Who is lying at this particular gate?
Back in the story, the rich man's failure wasn't one cruel choice against Lazarus. It was ordinary choices, day after day, made as if Lazarus weren't there.

how: Catholics live this through parish food pantries, the Society of St. Vincent de Paul, Catholic Charities and similar works, and through advocacy that asks how laws and budgets affect the poor.

games.q: what does “preferential option for the poor” mean?
o: a vow of poverty taken by friars and religious sisters
the belief that God loves poor people more than others
putting those in greatest need first in each decision

games.q: the option for the poor — tap the pairs.
p: the poor man at the gate
the first blessing on the plain
the poor who depend on others

s: the option for the poor means God loves the poor more than others
it's about who gets attention first, like a sick child at a family table. no one is loved less.
in Jesus' story, the poor man has a name and the rich man doesn't
the poor man is Lazarus; the rich man is only a certain rich man.
in the story, the rich man drives Lazarus away from his gate
the story doesn't say he does anything to Lazarus at all, or anything for him.

games.q: you're the poor man lying at the rich man's gate, hungry and covered in sores. what does the story say you long for?
o: the crumbs that fall from the table.
games.why: Lazarus wishes only for the crumbs from the rich man's table. the story's sting is how little he asks, and that no one gives it to him.

practice: Pick a decision in front of you this week: where to shop, how to vote on something, a rule at work, what to do with a little extra money.
Then walk around to the other side of the gate and ask who in your town has the least, and how this lands on them; you don't need to change your mind, just see from there for a moment.
If you pray, you can hold that person before God.

wordCard.voice: Preferential option for the poor. In Catholic teaching, the needs of the poor come first in judging any decision, the way a sick child is served first. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: poor, one who depends on others to live. Luke's word in "blessed are ye poor."

carryVoice: Your line: the poor first. The one in greatest need is served first, not loved more. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
